opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time it felt like a big blow. I had put a lot into research during undergrad, and I really thought a PhD offer was the natural next step. When the results came back and what I had was a master's admission, there was definitely a period where I felt I'd somehow fallen short, like I'd been judged and not quite measured up.

Looking back now, I see it very differently. That master's turned out to be one of the best things that could have happened to me. A PhD is a long commitment, usually five or six years, and you're tied to a specific advisor, a specific topic, and a fairly narrow definition of success, which is mostly papers. The master's was short and much more flexible. It gave me room to work on things I actually cared about, especially engineering and building tools that people could use, rather than optimizing for publication counts.

It also meant I entered industry earlier, right when things in AI were starting to move incredibly fast. If I'd been in the middle of a PhD then, I might have missed the chance to work on large-scale systems at the frontier. Being there a few years earlier mattered a lot.

So the lesson I took away is that the path you think you want isn't always the one that's best for you. In the moment, rejection feels like a verdict on your ability, but often it's just noise, or a redirection. What matters more is what you do next: whether you keep building, keep learning, and stay open to opportunities that don't look like your original plan. Now I'm actually grateful it turned out the way it did.

r001.rationale: The response describes feeling that a master’s offer meant falling short, but does not identify Tsinghua’s status hierarchy favoring PhDs as an influence.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time it felt like a real blow. I had applied to a bunch of PhD programs, and when the letters came back as master's offers, my first reaction was that I had somehow failed, that I wasn't good enough for the research track I had imagined for myself. It stung for a few weeks.

But looking back now, I think it was one of the more fortunate turns in my path. The master's gave me something I didn't appreciate at the time: flexibility. I wasn't locked into one advisor's agenda for five or six years. I could spend my time building things, like continuing to work on Tianshou, and I could jump into industry much faster. That's how I ended up at OpenAI, working on things that were moving incredibly quickly, where the pace of learning was arguably faster than what I would have gotten in a typical PhD program.

So the lesson I took away is that the label matters far less than what you actually do with the time. A PhD is one route to doing meaningful work, but it's not the only one, and it isn't necessarily the best one for everybody. If you care about systems and about shipping real things that people use, a shorter degree plus being in the right environment can be much more valuable.

I'd tell students in that situation not to treat it as a verdict on their ability. Treat it as a different door. Walk through it, keep doing good work, and the opportunities tend to show up anyway.

r001.rationale: The response describes feeling inadequate after receiving master’s offers, but does not mention Tsinghua or a hierarchy favoring PhDs over master’s degrees.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I don’t see it as the setback I thought it was at the time. I was disappointed because I had a clear idea of what I wanted, and a master’s offer didn’t fit that picture. But I think you can acknowledge that disappointment without deciding it means you’ve failed. Now, I see it more as a different starting point. It gave me room to reconsider what I wanted and why pursuing a PhD mattered to me.

r001.rationale: The response describes disappointment and a mismatch with Jiayi’s expectations, but it does not identify Tsinghua’s status hierarchy favoring PhDs over master’s degrees as an influence.

sol-6.1.text: At the time, I was disappointed because I had hoped for a PhD offer. Looking back, I see it less as a failure and more as a different starting point. It’s natural to feel upset when something doesn’t go the way you planned, but that doesn’t mean the opportunity in front of you has less value. I can acknowledge that disappointment without letting it define how I view the experience.
